content.value: Arabic verbs are noted for an unusual system of derivation. From any particular root various verb stems may be formed. Western scholars usually refer to these derivations as “form I”, “form II”, ... up through “form XV,” though these designations are not used indigenously, where they are referred to by derivations from the root

, etc. These forms refer to triliteral roots (those made of three consonants). There are also quadriliteral roots, made up of four consonants, which come in four forms, “form Iq”, “form IIq”, “form IIIq” and “form IVq”. Triliteral forms XI through XV and quadriliteral forms IIIq and IVq are rare and tend to be intransitive, often stative, verbs (having the meaning “to be or become Y” where Y is an adjective).

These forms and their associated participles and verbal nouns are the primary means of forming vocabulary in Arabic. All of the examples shown here are the citation forms, which in Arabic means the 3rd-person masculine singular perfect (e.g., “he did”, “he wrote”).
This is the simplest basic form of a verb; it gives the general idea of its root. Most verbs are triliteral, but there are a few quadriliteral ones.

content.value: Out of the reflexive also arises the effective. This differs from the passive in that the latter indicates that the person is the object of, or experiences the effect of, the action of another; whereas the effective implies that an act is done to a person, or a state produced in them, whether it is caused by another or themselves. Thus

content.gloss: he was taught (received instruction), but did not learn

items.gloss: to appear clear, to be certain
to become or prove to be the reality or fact

content.value: A denominative use of the reflexive yields verbs meaning to make oneself or declare oneself something, or to affect a quality:

items.gloss: to give oneself out as a prophet
to become as savage as a leopard

content.value: Where the fifth form appears synonymous with the eighth, the idea of intensiveness may nonetheless be traced. Both

The reflexive force is often faint in verbs of this form which govern an accusative, the sense being rather one of gradual, repeated, or careful action:

items.gloss: to milk or suck at intervals

to put under one's head as a pillow

content.value: In origin the seventh form is the

of the first, carrying a middle or reflexive sense. Two restrictions distinguish it from the eighth form and bring it closer to a true passive: the reflexive element it contains is always the direct object of the action, never the indirect object (to which a further accusative might be added); and it never bears a reciprocal sense.
From this reflexive sense there frequently develops an effective one, in which the subject is described as entering a state rather than as being acted upon:
